implementation_notes: The classic stateful filter is absorbed by the task-based API: each sub-request becomes a Task, Task.WhenAll completes when the last one arrives and returns the results in input order, so the wait-for-all aggregator collapses into a single await; when partials arrive independently of any task, keep them in a ConcurrentDictionary keyed by correlation id and complete a TaskCompletionSource when the count or deadline is reached. Reach for the classic collector shape whenever the completeness condition is not a fixed count - time-outs, first-best, external events, de-duplicated redelivery - because Task.WhenAll knows nothing about message identity and always awaits every task.
pitfalls: Task.WhenAll completes only when every task has finished; a faulted WhenAll task makes await rethrow one exception (its Exception still contains the aggregate), while the individual tasks retain any successful results - inspect them when partial tolerance is required.
Results come back in input order, not completion order: a first-best or time-out-with-override condition needs Task.WhenAny or a channel, not WhenAll.
Blocking on .Result/.Wait() instead of awaiting deadlocks when captured on a synchronization context (UI, legacy ASP.NET); keep the call chain async.

variants.name: TPL Dataflow BatchBlock pipeline
variants.implementation_notes: System.Threading.Tasks.Dataflow models the aggregator as a pipeline: BatchBlock<T> buffers incoming messages and emits one T[] as soon as its batch size - the completeness condition - is reached, and a linked ActionBlock merges and publishes. This is the .NET realization closest to the EIP intent for push-style arrival: buffering, back-pressure (BoundedCapacity) and completion propagation are the library's job rather than hand-written collector state. Use it when partials arrive from a channel or broker instead of from tasks you created; use Task.WhenAll when the fan-out is a fixed set of tasks you own.
pitfalls: BatchBlock emits full batches when the batch size is reached; one lost message stalls the expected group until a timer calls TriggerBatch() or a different completeness strategy is composed.
An unbounded BatchBlock buffers without limit; set BoundedCapacity and expect SendAsync to apply back-pressure.
Completion must be propagated (PropagateCompletion) and awaited, or the merge block is silently never completed and shutdown hangs.
